description: Most people are unaware of the abandoned equipment left in space. Our solution targets young children through an interactive 3D virtual world built into a website. Guided by our AI companion, "El Gatto," children can explore and interact with abandoned space equipment. The website connects to an ESP32 gaming console, where players use discovered rovers to fight aliens. Learning about real space equipment helps children unlock new game levels and abilities, making education fun and interactive.
summary:
Ask a kid what happens to a rover when its mission ends, and you’ll probably hear a movie plot. The real story is better. Machines from decades of missions are still sitting on the Moon and Mars, silent, right where they stopped, and each one changed what we know about the universe. Ghosts of Space brings them back to tell their stories.

Our 3D interactive website lets kids and teens explore the vehicles humanity left behind. They can spin, zoom, and inspect real 3D models, then dive into each vehicle’s story through real mission footage and see what it actually discovered. Every vehicle they learn about earns XP, so curiosity becomes progress.

The adventure doesn’t stop at the screen. Our custom-built console, shaped like our cat mascot El Gatto (yes, that’s our team name too), connects to the website and runs a mini-game. Players drive a rover across the Moon, collecting samples and dodging hazards.

Space isn’t magic. It’s engineering, patience, and discovery, and that’s exactly what makes it exciting.
details:
Brief description

Our project is a whole system that complements itself. It's divided, roughly, into three main parts: the 3D interactive website that has the rovers still left on the Moon and Mars, where the user can explore, inspect, and learn about each piece of equipment (except those that are NOT standing on any of the two surfaces), the video integrated with NASA's media (e.g., videos and sounds recorded of astronauts on these missions), with the voice narration performed by the team members telling the story of the rover, and a custom-made console with a playable game that was programmed using a 16-Megabytes ESP on a (128*160 pixels) screen.

The website includes quizzes about each rover after viewers watch the video and learn about it. When the player gets the quiz right, they receive a power-up in the console game. The score that the player gets is recorded on a leaderboard on the website for the database of all players. The player's XP on the website increases each time they learn about a rover.

(Technical details: Ghosts of Space is a React and TypeScript web app built with Vite. Its 3D worlds run on three.js and React Three Fiber, with custom shaders that render the Moon and Mars realistically from real NASA elevation data. A Node.js and Express backend stores progress in SQLite and talks to our ESP32 handheld console over WebSockets, while all mission content lives in validated JSON files.)

Descriptions about the rovers, alongside videos and sounds of astronauts, were retrieved from NASA's website. A demonstrated example of the usage of the website and one of the small videos for a rover is in the following video:

The console is programmed just one time using the Arduino IDE (C++ programming language). Then, it's put into its designed case (the cat mascot, El Gatto), which was 3D printed. It weighs 111 grams and was printed in about 3.5 hours. The console has a joystick and a button as the cat's eyes.

(Technical details: The cat mascot model was designed in Fusion 360 software)

Expected Impact

Ghosts of Space turns forgotten hardware into a reason to stay curious. By pairing real 3D models and mission footage with play, we expect kids and teens to leave with a more accurate picture of space research: slow, collaborative, built on engineering, and still producing knowledge long after a mission ends. The XP system and the El Gatto console give them a reason to come back, and every return means another vehicle learned. Because the website runs in any browser with no installation, science teachers can use it in class as a ready-made resource. To show real learning gains rather than assume them, we will measure understanding with a short quiz before and after the experience.

Further Recommendations

To reach a larger audience, the next step is expanding beyond the Moon and Mars to hardware across the solar system, such as Voyager in deep space and the Huygens probe on Titan. The stories should also be translated into Arabic and other languages. Partnerships with schools and science museums would bring the experience to students who would never find it alone, supported by a teacher dashboard with lesson plans and class leaderboards. Commercially, the website can stay free while revenue comes from selling the El Gatto console as an educational kit, licensing to schools and museums, and new mission packs.
